Ferrari, Lamborghini, Porsche: It's Time To Start Thinking About Rockets
41 photos
Photo: Tesla
Let's step back for a second and really look at what the all-new Tesla Roadster could bring to market once it enters production in about two years time. The fact that it can leap (instead of fly) like some early rendition of Superman, is nothing more than a distraction.
Try telling you wife enthusiastically how Tesla just unveiled a leaping, spinning car that people will be able to buy, and she’ll look at you as if you were a 14-year-old. Not that she doesn’t look at you like that already.
Sure, the fact that the Roadster can briefly take off and land is pretty wild. But it’s far from the bigger breakthrough here. For over a century, the car industry has struggled to generate as much grip as possible, using better tires, clever diffs, torque vectoring, just anything to improve acceleration. It’s usually the tires that limit performance. Just ask Mate Rimac or Christian von Koenigsegg.
What I see, when I look at the new Roadster , is possibility. Its cold-gas thrusters allow for a whole new way of applying force to a vehicle.
Rear-facing thrusters can generate forward momentum, but lateral thrusters could help a car change direction more efficiently. It’s properly fascinating. And I’d be way more impressed if the Tesla Roadster could achieve record levels of cornering speeds using controlled thrust, as opposed to performing wacky aerial stunts that benefit no one.
With that in mind, I think that this is the perfect time for the likes of Ferrari, Porsche, Lamborghini , and McLaren to develop their own thrust-assisted performance systems. Tesla doesn’t own that technology, because cold-gas thrusters aren’t anything new. Even a 12-year-old can understand the principle.
Gas is stored under high pressure and released through nozzles in whatever direction is deemed necessary. And because we’re talking about supercars and hypercars that already cost hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars, the additional expenses and complexity wouldn’t necessarily render such projects commercially impossible.
I’d like to see a thrust-assisted Porsche or Ferrari The first thing you need is the fan-based suction system. We know it works, because the Tesla Roadster isn’t the first automobile to use one. Any carmaker could implement such a technology, given enough resources.
Then come the lateral thrusters to generate sideways forces. This one is tricky, but possible – I mean, at this point, what is impossible?
Photo: Tesla Last but not least, the rear thrusters. Maybe you’ll use them as a sort of “push-to-pass”, or while having fun at the drag strip . I guess some forward-facing thrusters could help with braking, but now I’m just spitballing.
Like I said, in principle, any performance-oriented carmaker could copy and/or design variations of what Tesla just demonstrated. You can’t patent physics. Although, Tesla and SpaceX probably do have patents covering specific implementations, which is to be expected.
What I’d like to see from a breakthrough Porsche or Ferrari is something that uses small, precise thrust impulses to provide extra stability during extreme cornering, followed by an ultra-powerful burst of acceleration courtesy of the rear thrusters, coupled with the fan-based suction system.
Just put all that on the 2035 Porsche 911 GT3 RS and call it a day. Or in a new hypercar model. The latter is the more realistic scenario. I wonder if a thrust-assisted car would even qualify for all the currently viable production car lap records, or whether various motorsport entities would wake up feeling particularly litigious about it. That’s a conversation for another day.
Stop it, Sergiu, you’re losing it man! No. I. Am. Not. Is what I’d say using Ledger’s Joker voice. Here’s what you’re forgetting. BMW already demonstrated a fan suction system on the Vision Driving Experience prototype back in February of 2025. That thing had five electric impeller fans, generating roughly 1 ton of downforce even when the car was stationary. And then there’s the McMurtry Speirling, of course.
Photo: Tesla See, carmakers are already contemplating these things. They don’t need me to come up with any wild ideas – but they might need a kick in the rear from a rival brand, and that’s exactly what Tesla’s been known to do ever since they took the industry by storm with the original Model S.
What about the production Roadster? I don’t know. I won’t even speculate. I know some people think it won’t ever be allowed to leap in the air, and maybe it won’t. Or maybe you’ll only be able to do it under certain circumstances and in certain locations. I’m pretty sure you won’t be able to use it like a version of KITT’s turbo boost system , clearing traffic and other obstructions in the road.
Also, I’m not crazy about its styling. It’s a basic wedge-shaped, soulless sports car thingamajig, straight out of Cyberpunk or Blade Runner. I think we’ve had enough of these designs for a while.
